title: Meeting Bartok: 'Study Palestrina'
summary: Sauter's one meeting with Bartok and the lesson of spanning.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: He was a diminutive little man, Szegedi's blazing eyes. They were at Sagetti's apartment, rehearsing "Contrasty" and during an intermission I was introduced to Bartok, as a young composer, which I was. I was young anyway.
He didn't speak English very well. He looked at me with those eyes and said, "young man, study Palestrina." I tell that to everyone who is interested in writing, because I believe that.
If you look at what he did, he certainly did and if you look at what any of them did, they all did. There's no escaping it. The only time you don't sense that sort of thing is now.
What do you find, a kind of order the Palestrinas had?
It isn't quite that. It's how you span. I think the real lesson to learn is the spanning. It isn't the fact that it's counterpoint, which it
is, but it's also how to write melodies, how to make things balance, how you can make connections in that time span. It's not to be verbalized, at least I can't.
They knew something in those days and from that music came everything we have after that, although it itself is a result of something that happened before. It was sort of at the tail end of a--

A very strong period in western Europe at that time, and the whole thing comes as a result of Greek Roman culture too. It all comes from that, and if I think of not having that, as some critics would like to see, no thank you. I want it to be there for my life; I've had too much encouragement and real friendship from this, I would die without that stuff. And one day I will.
